title: Network Devices
summary: The fundamental building blocks of a network: routers, switches, firewalls, servers, and clients, and how they work together.

content.body:
A **computer network** is a digital communications network which allows nodes to share resources. A node is any device connected to the network. The simplest possible network is two PCs connected with a cable — once connected, they can exchange data.

This lesson introduces the five core device types you'll see everywhere in networking, and how they fit together.

nodes.label: Router
nodes.description: Forwards traffic between different networks and over the Internet.

nodes.label: Switch
nodes.description: Connects many end hosts within the same LAN.

nodes.label: Firewall
nodes.description: Controls traffic entering and exiting the network based on security rules.

nodes.label: Server
nodes.description: A device that provides functions or services for clients.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.description: A device that accesses a service made available by a server.

content.body:
Clients and servers are also called **end hosts** or **endpoints**.

- A **client** is a device that *accesses* a service made available by a server.
- A **server** is a device that *provides functions or services* for clients.

The two definitions are mirrors of each other. A laptop, desktop, or smartphone can be a client; a data-center machine running a web service can be a server.

**The same device can be a client in some situations and a server in others.** It is the *role* that matters, not the hardware.

sections.title: Client and server roles in action

steps.narration: PC1 requests the file image.jpg from PC2. PC1 is the device asking for a service.
PC2 responds and sends the file. PC2 is providing the service, so it is acting as the server.

content.body:
In network diagrams, a **cloud** is often used to represent the Internet, or any part of the network whose internal details aren't important to the current topic.

When your computer watches a video on YouTube, it sends a request that passes *through the Internet* to YouTube's servers. The reply comes back the same way — as a continuous stream of data until the video is done.

steps.narration: PC1 is in the New York branch LAN and SRV1 is in the Tokyo branch LAN. PC1 wants a file on SRV1.
PC1 sends the request to its switch SW1, which forwards it to R1.
R1 forwards the request over the Internet to R2.
R2 sends it via SW2 to SRV1. Switches carry traffic within a LAN; routers carry traffic between LANs.
The reply follows the reverse path back to PC1.

content.body:
**Switches**
- Provide connectivity to hosts *within the same LAN* (e.g. all the PCs on one office floor, or your home network).
- Have many interfaces (often 24 or more) to connect end hosts.
- Do *not* provide connectivity between LANs or over the Internet.

**Routers**
- Provide connectivity *between* LANs.
- Have relatively few network interfaces compared to switches.
- Send data over the Internet.

Cisco Catalyst switches (e.g. Catalyst 9200, 3650) are Cisco's enterprise-grade switches. Cisco ISR 1000/4000/900 series are common enterprise routers.

A **firewall** is a specialty security device that controls traffic entering and exiting the network, based on **configured rules** that define which traffic is allowed and which is denied.

- Firewalls can be placed **outside** the router (filtering traffic before it reaches the router) or **inside** the network (after the router), or both.
- A **network firewall** is a hardware appliance that filters traffic *between networks* — this is the type the CCNA focuses on.
- A **host-based firewall** is software on a single machine (like the firewall on your PC). Even with a hardware firewall, each PC should run one as an extra line of defense.
- A **next-generation firewall** adds more advanced filtering capabilities (e.g. intrusion prevention) on top of traditional firewall features. Cisco examples: ASA 5500-X and Firepower 2100 series.

content.body: When a question describes connecting *many end hosts in the same location*, the answer is a **switch**. When it describes connecting *separate networks together*, the answer is a **router**. When it asks about *monitoring and controlling traffic in and out*, the answer is a **firewall**.

questions.question: Your company wants to purchase network hardware to which they can connect the 30 PCs in your department. Which type of network device is appropriate?
questions.explanation: A router is designed for forwarding traffic between networks, not for connecting many end hosts, and typically won't have 30 interfaces. A firewall filters traffic entering/exiting the local network and isn't designed to connect directly to end hosts. A server is an end host itself. A switch is designed to connect many end hosts within the same LAN and has many network interfaces.

questions.question: You received a video file from your friend's Apple iPhone using AirDrop. What was his iPhone functioning as in that transaction?
questions.explanation: A client accesses a service, it does not provide a service. An end host like an iPhone doesn't function as a LAN by itself, though it can be part of one. A server is a device that provides functions or services for clients — your friend's phone provided the file, so it functioned as a server.

questions.question: What is your computer or smartphone functioning as while you watch this video?
questions.explanation: Your device is receiving a service, not providing one, so it is not a server. Although it is an end host, that doesn't describe its function — both servers and clients are end hosts. Since it is receiving a service from YouTube's servers, it is functioning as a client.

questions.question: Your company wants to purchase network hardware to connect its separate networks together. What kind of network device is appropriate?
questions.explanation: Although a firewall can connect multiple networks, its real purpose is to monitor and control traffic entering and exiting. 'Host' can refer to any network node, and a LAN is not a device at all. A router is designed to connect and forward traffic between multiple networks.

questions.question: Your company wants to upgrade its old network firewall to one that provides more advanced functions. What kind of firewall should they purchase?
questions.explanation: A host-based firewall runs on an end host and is not a network firewall. 'Next-level' and 'top-layer' are not actual firewall types. A next-generation firewall combines traditional firewall features with more advanced filtering capabilities.
